A shirtwaist is a woman's top — specifically a blouse that is cut and styled to look like a man's dress shirt. Think of the classic men's button-up shirt you might picture on a businessman: a collar at the neck, a row of buttons running straight down the front, and cuffs at the wrists. Now imagine that same design made for a woman's body. That is a shirtwaist.---

A shirtwaist has a few defining physical features:

  • A collar — usually a stiff, upright or fold-down collar, just like a dress shirt.
  • Buttons down the front — typically running from the collar to the waist.
  • Long sleeves with cuffs — though shorter sleeves were also made.
  • A fitted or semi-fitted body — it hugs or follows the shape of the torso.
  • It was almost always worn tucked into a long skirt, with the waistband of the skirt sitting over the bottom of the blouse. The two pieces together — blouse and skirt — formed a complete outfit.

What made the shirtwaist distinctive is that it borrowed masculine shirt design and applied it to women's clothing. Before this, women's tops (called "bodices") were often heavily decorated, structured with stays (boning), and difficult to move in. The shirtwaist was comparatively plain, practical, and easy to wear — almost businesslike.

The shirtwaist had its golden age roughly between 1890 and 1920, especially in the United States. During this period, more women were entering the workforce — working in offices, shops, and factories — and they needed clothing that was practical, washable, and affordable. The shirtwaist answered all of these needs perfectly.

It became the go-to outfit for the working woman of that era. If you look at photographs of American women from the early 1900s — especially women in offices or on city streets — most of them are wearing a shirtwaist tucked into a long, full skirt. It was so universal that it became almost a uniform of the era. Fashion historians often see the shirtwaist as a symbol of women's growing independence and entry into public life during that period.

Over time, the design evolved. Instead of a separate blouse worn with a skirt, designers began making one-piece dresses where the top half was styled exactly like a shirtwaist — with the collar, button-front, and fitted bodice — and a skirt was attached at the waist. This garment is called a shirtwaist dress (or sometimes a "shirt dress").

The shirtwaist dress became enormously popular through the mid-20th century, particularly in the 1940s and 1950s. It had a cinched or defined waist, a full or straight skirt flowing below, and that characteristic button-down front. It looked polished but was easy to wear — the kind of dress a woman might wear to work, to a casual lunch, or around the house. It became one of the most iconic silhouettes in 20th-century women's fashion.---
An important historical connection: The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire

You cannot fully understand this word without knowing about one of history's most significant industrial disasters. In March 1911, a fire broke out at the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory in New York City — a garment factory where mostly young immigrant women worked long hours in cramped, unsafe conditions making shirtwaist blouses. The factory owners had locked several of the exit doors (to prevent workers from taking unauthorized breaks), and when the fire started, 146 workers died — many of them burned, and many others who jumped from the upper-floor windows to their deaths.

The disaster shocked the American public. It directly led to major labor law reforms: stricter safety regulations, better fire codes, limits on working hours, and stronger labor unions. The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire is one of the defining events in the history of workers' rights in America, and the word "shirtwaist" is permanently connected to it.
Is the word still used today?

As a word for a standalone blouse, "shirtwaist" is largely old-fashioned today. If you are describing that type of top in modern conversation, you would most likely just call it a blouse or a button-down shirt. The word "shirtwaist" by itself sounds dated and is mainly found in historical writing, old literature, or fashion history texts.

However, the term "shirtwaist dress" (or "shirt dress") is still alive and commonly used in fashion. The style itself — a dress with a button-front top and a defined waist — has never truly gone out of fashion. Designers revisit it in every decade, and you can easily find shirt dresses in clothing stores today.

ConceptWhat to know

A shirtwaist is a woman's blouse designed to look like a man's shirt — with a collar, buttons down the front, and cuffs. It was the essential everyday garment for working women around 1890–1920. When the same design was built into a one-piece dress (with a skirt attached), it became the shirtwaist dress, which remained a fashion staple well into the 20th century. The word is also permanently tied to the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire of 1911, a tragedy that changed American labor laws. Today, the word itself is somewhat archaic, but the style of dress it inspired is still very much around.
